mcqs.question: How does an 'undecidable' problem differ from an 'NP-hard' problem?
options: NP-hard problems are solvable but believed to require exponential time; undecidable problems have no algorithm at all, for any amount of time
They're the same thing, just different names used by different textbooks
Undecidable problems are a subset of NP-hard problems
NP-hard means 'impossible to solve'; undecidable means 'slow to solve'
mcqs.explanation: NP-hard problems (like TSP) are decidable — an algorithm exists and will eventually give the correct answer, it just may take exponential time in the worst case. Undecidable problems (like the halting problem) have no correct algorithm whatsoever, regardless of how much time is allowed. These are different axes entirely (solvability vs. efficiency), not variations of the same idea.

mcqs.question: In the diagonalization proof of the halting problem, why does constructing D(P) — which does the opposite of what H predicts — prove that H can't exist?
options: Because D(D) is undefined and therefore the proof doesn't actually work
Because asking whether D(D) halts leads to a contradiction no matter what H(D,D) answers, so no correct H can exist
Because D always halts, which contradicts the definition of a Turing machine
Because H can simply refuse to answer for D, avoiding the contradiction
mcqs.explanation: The construction forces a contradiction in both cases: if H predicts D(D) halts, D is built to loop instead; if H predicts D(D) loops, D is built to halt instead. Since H must give one of these two answers and both lead to H being wrong, no consistently correct H can exist. A halting-checker is assumed total (must answer for every input), so 'refusing to answer' isn't an option available to H by the problem's own definition.

mcqs.question: A static-analysis tool flags a loop as 'possibly infinite' with a note that it might be wrong in either direction. Given that the halting problem is undecidable, is this design choice a flaw the tool's authors should fix?
options: Yes, a well-designed tool should always give a definite yes/no answer for every loop

No — this is the correct, deliberate design: since no algorithm can decide halting for every possible program, real tools use conservative approximations that accept some false positives/negatives rather than claim impossible certainty
Yes, the tool should just run the program to completion instead of analyzing it statically
No, but only because current hardware isn't fast enough yet — a sufficiently fast computer could solve this correctly for every program
mcqs.explanation: Because the halting problem is provably undecidable for the general case, any tool that claimed perfect certainty for every program would be claiming something mathematically impossible — the correct, deliberate engineering choice is a conservative approximation that sometimes says 'can't determine' or accepts some error. This isn't a speed limitation (more hardware can't fix an impossibility result), and 'just run it' fails for genuinely non-terminating programs.

mcqs.question: In the reduction proving 'does program P ever print hello' is undecidable, why does the constructed program Q print 'hello' if and only if P(x) halts?
options: Because Q is defined to run P(x) first and only reach its own print statement once that call returns, so the print happens exactly when P(x) finishes
Because Q always prints 'hello' regardless of what P(x) does
Because PrintsHello(Q) is assumed to always return true by definition
Because Q modifies P(x) to force it to halt early
mcqs.explanation: Q is constructed to call P(x) and place the 'hello' print immediately after that call — control only reaches the print statement if P(x) actually returns (halts); if P(x) runs forever, Q never gets to the print at all. This tight correspondence is exactly what lets PrintsHello(Q) stand in for 'does P halt on x,' without modifying P's behavior or assuming any particular answer in advance.
